name: Umar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in an office on the retail park by the ring road, six of us. Our big clients are three car dealerships and a tyre chain, so it's web banners, showroom posters and a lot of 'zero percent finance' in big red letters. I've got AI tools set up for nearly everything: I feed in the car photo and the offer, get twenty layouts, and spend my time fixing the hands and the logos it mangles.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about that, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being fast, and Karen, my boss, has noticed. The hard bit is I'm still not a strong designer underneath, my type and colour choices are basic. And money, obviously: I'm on junior pay, I've got about a week and a half saved, and my partner Ines is a receptionist at a dental practice, so no one's rich in our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I called it, it's a handy tool, not magic. I'd still tell people to use it, because it saves me hours. I'd post a few before-and-after examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my small edge. I'm the one who's fastest with the tools at the agency, and that stays useful. But it doesn't fix the pay, and car dealers cut their ad spend whenever sales drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and try to get better at the actual design underneath, maybe a colour theory course. I'd keep doing YouTube thumbnails for gamers on the side, that's about a hundred and fifty a month. I'd put that straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Slightly bored, honestly, I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said dealers cut spend when sales drop. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it has. When car sales dropped last winter, two of our dealerships halved their ad budgets overnight, and my overtime disappeared with them. Karen didn't cut anyone, but she stopped paying overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the agency you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, who does the print proofing and file checks. Even a small tool takes some of that. She's been there twelve years and she's nervous of all of it.

think: I keep my **small edge** as the fastest tool user at the agency.
Car dealers **cut ad spend** whenever sales drop, which hits my hours.
do: Take a **colour theory** course to improve the design underneath.
Keep making **YouTube thumbnails** for about a hundred and fifty a month.
Put the thumbnail money straight into **savings**.
feel: **Fine**, but slightly **bored**, because I like things moving.

steps.text: Take an online colour theory course this winter
Keep making YouTube thumbnails for gamers on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn, not to moan. I'd run a lunchtime session at the agency showing everyone my setup. Online I'd share my workflows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the people who comes out okay. Karen will want fewer designers and one person who can run the tools across all the clients. If my boss can only keep one junior, she'll keep the one who already runs the tools across all our clients, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Karen to make me the agency's tools lead, with a small raise, in the next six months. I'd build templates for each dealership so we can turn around a sale weekend in an hour. I'd keep the thumbnails going in case I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, mostly excited. It's my kind of world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in case you're wrong. What would wrong look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wrong is the dealerships doing it themselves. Their marketing managers can type a prompt too. Then it's not about whether I'm fast, it's whether we're needed at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines's job worries me more than mine, honestly. Booking and reminder calls are exactly what these tools do. I'd tell her to start looking at the dental nurse course.

do: Ask Karen to make me **tools lead** with a raise within six months.

fieldNote: He's confident, but admits the risk of **clients going direct**.
He worries more for **his partner's job** in booking and reminders.
His plan is to **become indispensable** within the agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody is ready for this, including me. I'd say governments need to act now on income support. I'd stop telling people to learn tools, because it wouldn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my whole advantage is being good with AI, and in this world AI doesn't need me to be good with it. Everything I do is screen work, so 2028 finishes it. Ines's reception job goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every penny out of the next two years: extra thumbnails, freelance banners for anyone. I'd look at the dealership's workshop, valeting or tyre fitting, because that's hands-on until about 2031. We'd move somewhere cheaper, maybe share with my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I trained for the wrong race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been upbeat until now. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being the fastest person with AI is worth nothing once the AI doesn't need a person at all. In the slower picture I'm ahead; here, everybody is behind, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the thumbnail side income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gone too, probably. Gamers would make their own in two seconds. I'd be living on whatever I could do with my hands.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready**, including me.
I'd push for **income support** instead of telling people to learn tools.
think: My edge with AI is **worthless** once AI needs no operator.
Both my job and **Ines's reception** job end around 2028.
do: Earn **extra money** from thumbnails and freelance banners for two years.
Ask the dealership workshop about **valeting or tyres**.
Move in with **my brother** to cut rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, like I **trained** for the wrong race.
S2.quote: Being the fastest person with AI is worth nothing once the AI doesn't need a person at all.
fieldNote: His **optimism collapses** when AI no longer needs an operator.
Both household earners do **thinking work**, so both are hit in 2028.
He'd move to **hands-on car work** for the robot gap.

steps.text: Take every freelance banner and thumbnail job for two years
Ask the dealership workshop about valeting or tyre fitting
Move in with his brother to cut rent
Stop all spending beyond rent, food and phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's be smart. I'd still say learn the tools, but also learn something solid. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd ride the tools wave for three years or so, and probably earn more than now. But I'd be building the exit at the same time, because 2031 still ends my job. I'd want something hands-on in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be tools lead now and get the raise. With that money I'd do an evening course in vehicle wrapping, it's design plus hands-on, so it lasts until the robots. Ines would start her dental nurse training this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in control. It feels like a game I can play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why vehicle wrapping in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wrapping a car is design you have to do with your hands, with a heat gun and a squeegee, so it lasts until the robots come. And the dealerships already know me, so I've got customers on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The raise goes into savings, not the car. I want three months saved by 2028. That's never happened in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case if it has to come. Ten years is enough to sort yourself out. I'd tell young designers to start now anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd have years of being the tools person, then a decent move before 2036. I'd probably set up my own small wrap and signs business by 2030. I'd be 37 when AGI lands, with my own customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become tools lead, save hard for three years, and then buy a used plotter and heat gun for wrapping, about four thousand. I'd do wraps on weekends first. I'd keep my eye on the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly optimistic. I like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you nervous, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long, but the junior design jobs start disappearing in year two or three, not year ten, so I can't relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you need anyone's help to start the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe my brother, he's a mechanic and has a garage space we could use. Family first, before a bank loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole edge vanishes and Ines's job goes too. What would help is some income support for a couple of years, and cheap loans for small hands-on businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the guy who brought the tools in. I showed everyone at my agency how to use AI, and in the fast version I basically trained the thing that replaces us.

headlineQuote: I showed everyone at my agency how to use AI, and in the fast version I basically trained the thing that replaces us.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old junior** designer making car dealership ads on a retail park.
He uses AI **every day** and is the fastest at his agency, though his design basics are weak.
His partner Ines is a **dental receptionist**, and they have under two weeks saved.
He is **upbeat** with slow change but **alarmed** by fast AGI.
His long plan is a **vehicle wrapping** business with his brother's garage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, ending both his and Ines's job at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** for two years and **cheap loans** for small hands-on businesses.
